extracted.intended_audience: Presbyterian ministers, church judicatories, and adherents concerned with covenanted Presbyterian doctrine and polity (early-18th-century Scotland/Ireland)
extracted.subtask_short: Presbyterian testimony against church and state
extracted.subtask_description: A judicial Presbytery testimony enumerating grounds to disapprove of the established Church and State: doctrinal failures, moral/disciplinary laxity, improper civil–ecclesiastical relations, and the scriptural requirements for magistracy. It both accuses specific persons/parties and sets out the normative standards the Presbytery believes ought to be followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate censure for proven heresy
rubrics_metrics.description: When ministers or members are 'processed before her assemblies, and convicted of maintaining many gross errors', adequate censure must be inflicted rather than gentle admonition or dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Mr. Simpson (convicted of Arminian, Socinian, Pelagian and Arian errors but dismissed with a gentle admonition), Mr. Campbell and others; the lack of adequate censure is presented as proof of the church's corruption and unfaithfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm condemnation of particular heresies (Arminian, Pelagian, Arian, Socinian)
rubrics_metrics.description: The church must publicly condemn and judicially oppose doctrinal systems that deny essential gospel truths (e.g., denial of Christ's necessary existence or the numerical oneness of the Trinity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text urges the church to vindicate 'the precious truths of Christ' when they are impugned; failure to do so (e.g., Simpson's denial of Christ's deity being insufficiently punished) demonstrates unsoundness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting antinomian mischaracterisation of gospel truths
rubrics_metrics.description: The church ought not to condemn sound gospel truths (such as believers' freedom from the law as a covenant of works) as 'gross antinomian errors'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The condemnation of 'The marrow of modern divinity' as antinomian is criticized as condemning 'many great gospel truths', opening the door to legalistic teaching and Baxterian principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent propagation of heterodox teaching by ministers and professors
rubrics_metrics.description: Heads of colleges, professors, and ministers must not recommend, teach, or otherwise propagate books or sermons that promote heterodox principles; recommending such works is evidence of unsoundness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: recommendation of Doctor Whitchcot's sermons by Mr. Wishart after being assoilzied; Leechman's 'Christless' sermon on prayer being extolled and the author dismissed without proper rebuke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline and exclusion for those promoting independent/anti-presbyterian church government
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who preach and print independent schemes of church government, deny the warrant for national churches under the New Testament, or set up independent congregations should be suspended/depoded and not reponed if unrepentant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case of Mr. Glas and others: initially suspended and deposed, later reponed despite no remorse, then they set up independent churches and ordained mechanics; such leniency is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and emit faithful warnings and public testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Church judicatories should publicly assert and affirm precious truths, emit solemn warnings about dangerous doctrines, and 'lift up the faithful standard of a judicial testimony' when errors are prevalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Presbytery complains that necessary public warnings have been 'contemned and disregarded' despite repeated representations reminding the church of this duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: No excessive lenity toward gross heretics
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive, sinful lenity toward gross heretics (allowing them to remain ministers/members without renouncing heterodox principles) is itself a mark of unsoundness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cases (Simpson, Campbell, Wishart, Leechman) are offered where lenient treatment encouraged further error and the spread of heresy among students and congregations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testify against toleration/indulgence principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Toleration or indulgence footing (e.g., royal indulgence/toleration acts as a basis for Presbyterian settlement) is regarded as anti-scriptural and to be testified against.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Presbytery views Irish 'Presbyterians' who rely on indulgence as disavowing true Presbyterianism and therefore warns against toleration as an anti-scriptural shelter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warn the people against 'Newlight' and poisonous medleys of error
rubrics_metrics.description: Public exhortation to the people to beware of men and books spreading 'Newlight' (a 'poisonous jumble' of errors) and to seek the true knowledge of Christ's gospel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Presbytery 'judicially warn and exhort' the people in Ireland to avoid such men and to be established in gospel truth, citing Eph. iv.14–15 as a charge against being 'tossed to and fro' with every wind of doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose sinful associations of church and state with malignants
rubrics_metrics.description: Both church and state should be testified against when they associate with declared enemies of the covenanted interest (malignants), admit them to civil office, or enter alliances with idolators and persecutors of Protestant interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: civil laws requiring renunciation of covenantal friendship to hold office; praying for allied armies composed largely of 'Popish idolaters'; approving union with England; acknowledging the civil power of church men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress impiety, vice, and superstition — enactment and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil and ecclesiastical authorities ought to suppress impiety, vice, and superstitious observance of holy days; mere laws are insufficient without vigorous execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text faults the state for tolerating stage-plays, masquerades, balls, and for allowing courts to stand down on holy-days; also criticizes ministers' attendance at such events as scandalous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject Erastian subjection of ecclesiastical power to civil power
rubrics_metrics.description: The ecclesiastical power must not be subjected to the civil magistrate (Erastianism); putting the ecclesiastical under civil authority and making ministers mere inspectors/informers is anti-scriptural and dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Presbytery argues that subjecting church government to civil authority and making ministers the 'bare inspectors of men's manners' will not be blessed by God and will bring judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistracy must be divinely instituted and conform to scriptural qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawful magistracy is a divine ordinance: authority must be 'of God' (both institution and constitution), and magistrates must meet scriptural qualifications (fear of God, wisdom, integrity), not merely be the product of popular will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive scriptural support is cited (e.g., Exod. xviii.21; Deut. xvii.14–15; Prov. xxiv.21; 1 Cor. vi.1,4–5) to show that God prescribes qualifications and that people are limited in choice by divine rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: People's choice alone insufficient to constitute lawful magistracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere inclination or choice of the people cannot alone make a lawful magistrate if the person fails to satisfy divine, scriptural requirements for the office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Presbytery rejects the Seceders' claim that the people are the 'ultimate fountain of magistracy' without regard to qualifications; argues that more is required than popular recognition to make a power 'ordained of God.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural character requirements for rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Those raised to rule must be 'able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness'; a man 'in whom is the spirit' (spirit of wisdom/government), known integrity, and affection to the welfare of God's people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: Exod. xviii.21; Numb. xxvii.18; Deut. i.13; Deut. xvii.14–15; 2 Sam. xxiii.2–4; Job xxxiv.17–18 to ground these character requirements as both scriptural precept and limit on popular choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denounce and (where appropriate) punish authors of atheistical/antitrinitarian principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and promulgators of antitrinitarian, atheistical, or blasphemous principles (e.g., David Hume, 'Sopho') deserve strong censure and, where civil law so provides, punishment; the church/state should act to suppress such tenets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although civil laws declared such positions criminal and capital, the Presbytery laments that civil powers have not punished authors; failure to act is part of the church/state's negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful testimony must involve reproving all ranks and sins
rubrics_metrics.description: The church must 'maintain suitable testimony against sins of all sorts, in persons of all stations,' issuing faithful warnings and clear declarations of present duty irrespective of the social rank of offenders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Presbytery criticizes the Revolution Church for making 'a formal concert... binding up one another from preaching against, and applying their doctrines to the sins, corruptions and scandals of the times.'
